title: Can four be worth more than seven?
objective: Explain why a digit can contribute more than a larger digit because of its place.
successEvidence: The learner compares tenths and hundredths using the same whole and explains a new example in words.

steps.title: Keep the whole fixed
steps.body: One strip contains ten of the small cells. The outside square has not changed, so one strip is one tenth and each small cell is one hundredth.

steps.title: Compare with the same-sized pieces
steps.body: A tenth is ten times the size of a hundredth. Convert both contributions to hundredths before comparing them.

steps.title: The 4 contributes forty hundredths
steps.body: In 3.47, the 4 is in the tenths place. Four full strips contain forty hundredth cells.

steps.title: The 7 contributes seven hundredths
steps.body: Seven small cells do not fill one complete tenth. Forty hundredths are greater than seven hundredths, so the 4 contributes more.

steps.title: Name the unit, not only the digit
steps.body: The first place after the decimal point is tenths. The second is hundredths. In 2.63, the 3 is three hundredths, written 0.03.

steps.title: The zero holds the tenths place
steps.body: 0.6 is six tenths, or sixty hundredths. 0.06 is only six hundredths. The zero changes the place of the 6.

steps.title: Digit tells how many; place tells which unit
steps.body: When you explain a decimal digit, name both the number of units and whether those units are tenths or hundredths.

checks.prompt: One whole is split into 100 equal cells. How many cells make one tenth?
checks.successMessage: Ready. One tenth is ten hundredths of the same whole.
checks.explanationPrompt: Tell someone why the outside square must stay the same size.

choices.feedback: One cell is one hundredth. Look at how many cells fill a complete strip.
choices.misconception: Confuses one tenth with one hundredth

choices.feedback: One hundred cells make the whole, not one tenth.
choices.misconception: Treats the whole as one tenth

checks.prompt: In 2.63, what value does the 3 contribute?
checks.successMessage: Yes. The 3 is in the hundredths place, so it contributes 0.03.
checks.explanationPrompt: Explain using both the digit and its place.

choices.feedback: That names the digit as ones. Check which side of the decimal point it is on.
That would be true in 2.36. In 2.63, the 3 is in the second decimal place.

checks.successMessage: Correct. Six tenths equal sixty hundredths, which is greater than six hundredths.
checks.explanationPrompt: Explain the comparison without saying only that one number has fewer digits.

choices.feedback: More written digits do not make a decimal larger. Convert both to hundredths.
choices.misconception: Compares decimal strings like whole numbers

choices.feedback: The same digit can represent different values in different places.
choices.misconception: Attends to the digit but not its place

checks.prompt: Tomorrow: which digit contributes more in 2.39—the 3 or the 9?
checks.successMessage: Correct. Three tenths equal thirty hundredths, so the 3 contributes more than the 9.
checks.explanationPrompt: Explain by converting both contributions to hundredths.

choices.feedback: Nine is the larger digit, but its place makes it nine hundredths. Compare 30 hundredths with 9 hundredths.
choices.misconception: Assumes the larger digit always contributes more

choices.feedback: They use different units: tenths and hundredths.
choices.misconception: Treats tenths and hundredths as equal-sized units
